subtopic: BILL TO FACILITATE COMPROMISES AND ARRANGEMENTS IN CASES OF INSOLVENCY

speechtext:
Hon. O. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 77, to facilitate compromises and arrangements between companies and their creditors.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at the present time any company in Canada, whether it be organized under the laws of the Dominion of Canada or under the laws of any of the provinces of Canada, which becomes bankrupt or insolvent is thereby brought under either the Bankruptcy Act or the Winding-up Act. These acts provide for the liquidation of the company under a trustee in bankruptcy in the one case and under a liquidator in the other, and the almost inevitable result is that the organization of the company is entirely disrupted, its good-will depreciated and ultimately lost, and the balance of the assets sold by the trustees or the liquidator for whatever they will bring. There is no mode or method under our laws whereby the creditors of a

Companies and Creditors
company may be brought into court and permitted by amicable agreement between themselves to arrange for a settlement or compromise of the debts of the company in such a way as to permit the company effectively to continue its business by its reorganization. Sections 144 and 145 of the Companies Act of Canada provide that the shareholders of a company may meet to adjust the relationship between classes of shares in the company. Several of the provincial acts also contain provisions whereby the shareholders may meet to make compromises and arrangements between the shareholders. Under the British North America Act, bankruptcy and insolvency fall exclusively within the legislative jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada.
At the present time some legal method of making arrangements and compromises between creditors and companies is perhaps more necessary because of the prevailing commercial and industrial depression, and it was thought by the government that we should adopt some method whereby compromises might be carried into effect under the supervision of the courts without utterly destroying the company or its organization, without loss of good-will and without forcing the improvident sale of its assets. Therefore, we have studied carefully the provisions of the English Companies Act of 1929. This act contains a provision to permit such compromises and arrangements with creditors and I should like to read section 153 of that act upon which this bill is based. It reads:
153.

(1) Where a compromise or arrangement is proposed between a company and its creditors or any class of them, or between the company and its members or any class of them, the court may, on the application in a summary way of the company or of any creditor or member of the company, or, in the case of a company being wound up, of the liquidator, order a meeting of the creditors or class of creditors, or of the members of the company or class of members, as the case may be, to be summoned in such manner as the court directs.
(2) If a majority in number representing three-fourths in value of the creditors or class of creditors, or members or class of members, as the case may be, present and voting either in person or by proxy at the meeting, agree to any compromise or arrangement, the compromise or arrangement shall, if sanctioned by the court, be binding on all the creditors or the class of creditors, or on the members or class of members, as the ease may be, and also on the company or, in the case of a company in the course of being w-ound up, on the liquidator and contributories of the company.
In attempting to draft an act which will certainly be within the legislative competence of the parliament of Canada we felt that we should not seemingly entrench upon provincial jurisdiction so far as to provide for compromises between classes of shareholders of provincial companies, and therefore we have provided in this bill, which I am about to introduce, that the provincial law shall apply in respect of provincial companies in so far the the compromise may affect the shareholders, but we provide also for the convening of a meeting of creditors of any company which is bankrupt or insolvent under supervision of the court, so that, if possible, an amicable compromise or arrangement may be arrived at; and, in so far as such compromise or arrangement may necessitate with respect to provincial companies compromises or arrangements between classes of shareholders we have authorized the court to proceed conjointly under this proposed act and the provincial acts for the purpose of convening meetings of shareholders or classes of shareholders.
The bill as drafted is quite simple. It seems to the government very necessary that such a measure should be introduced, and I commend it to the careful consideration of the members of the house.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. MURRAY MaeLAREN (Minister of Pensions and National Health) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:

Pension Act
That it is expedient to amend the Pension Act to give effect to certain recommendations of the committee appointed to investigate the administration of the act; to provide for the elimination of various provisions relating to the pension tribunal; and for an increase in the number of members of the commission and to prescribe their tenure of office; for the continuation of the pension appeal court as a court of appeal and of review; for the appointment of an ad hoc judge as a member of the pension appeal court and his remuneration; for the appointment of a travelling _ inspector of the veterans' bureau, and of pension counsel, and a reviewing officer; for the payment of awards by the comptroller of the treasury, and generally to simplify and improve procedure under the act.

Explain.
Mr. MacLAREN; I wish to take this opportunity of making a preliminary statement regarding the resolution which we have just heard read from the chair, perhaps not in any detail for it is probably the wish of the house that the subject matter of the resolution should be more fully explained at a later stage.
The resolution proposes certain amendments to the Pension Act. The amendments relate especially to a certain portion of the Pension Act, namely, that dealing with its administration. In September of last year the government appointed a special committee to inquire into the administration of the Pension Act. It was composed in all of eleven members. Five were representatives of veterans' organizations, five were representatives of the different branches of the Department of Pensions and National Health, and Mr. Justic Rinfret of the Supreme Court of Canada acted as chairman. So far as I am aware the committee was composed differently from any I previously recall. It met in Ottawa, and over a period of about six weeks heard witnesses from various parts of Canada, after which a final report was submitted to the government. During the course of the meetings it was found that on account of the urgent necessity of his attendance to duties in the Supreme court, the chairman could not continue to act. Mr. Justice Audette took his place, and completed the duties which fell to the chairman of the committee.
The report of the committee was submitted in three parts. While in matters of detail there are indications of some division of opinion, yet in connection with larger and more important matters there is substantial agreement. I am making a general statement, and am not speaking absolutely. I believe I am speaking correctly however when I state that in connection with important matters of
principle there is general agreement. The reference to the committee, in the terms of the order in council, was to examine and report on the administration of the Pension Act. Since that time the report has been printed and distributed to hon. members.
The appointment of the committee, and the hearings before it were due, to a great extent, to representations made to the government by allied organizations, to the effect that there was dissatisfaction due to delay in making decisions, congestion in the different courts, and an undue number of appeals to the pension appeal court. There were other troubles, but I believe I have indicated the three chief ones. The attention of the committee was directed naturally, to the special conditions about which complaint had been made. The resolution now before us sets out the nature of the amendments proposed, and in connection with which I shall mention briefly the more important features.
At the present time there are three adjudicating bodies administering the Pension Act. There is the board of pension commissioners, the pension tribunal and the pension appeal court. Under the amendment it is proposed that there be only two adjudicating bodies, namely the board of pension commissioners and the pension appeal court. Under these circumstances the pension tribunal, which has been functioning for a few years and still functions, will cease to operate. On the other hand there will be an increase in the personnel of the board of pension commissioners. Then there will be provision for the enlargement of the pension appeal court, if necessary. In any case it will be arranged so that there may be two courts sitting at the same time in order to expedite and dispose of the business. One of the essential features of the pension tribunal has been preserved, namely that a quorum of two shall be what one might term a travelling board, so that when necessary those quorums may proceed through the country acting as travelling boards, as now obtains under the tribunal. Secondly, those boards will have the right to make a decision. The two essential features of the tribunal as it now exists will be safeguarded and preserved.
There are one or two further points which I might mention before moving the adoption of the resolution. The first is in regard to the reviewing officer. The objection has been taken frequently in the house that the official or officials who take appeals should not be subject to the pension board or to the minister. The provision which will appear in the bill is that this officer, known as the reviewing officer, shall first be a medical man so that
Pension Act

he may determine on questions of disability. On his advice appeals shall or shall not be taken. Secondly, he is to receive direction from the president of the appeal court.

That is
only in regard to crown appeals.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I am speaking of cases
upon which decisions have been made favourable to the applicant. Of course applicants who have not been successful are always at liberty within a certain time to take an appeal.
I think possibly the house has heard enough of the details now, I would like to make this general statement, that there are a number of provisions, of amendments, which will I think go far to expedite and simplify the machinery, so that matters can move more rapidly in the future. There will be less delay. Personally I recognize that there has been delay. I do not hold the officials responsible for it, I regard the impossible amount of work as the essential cause. In any case the amendments will have the effect of disposing of thousands of cases that are almost dormant yet cannot be removed. Applicants who are not taking further action will be communicated with, will be given ample time to express their views as to whether or not they desire to proceed, and if they are not proceeding then their cases will be removed. In this way much will be done, I feel, to clear up the work more promptly and satisfactorily. This will go far towards disposing of the complaints that have been made, especially as regards delays in giving decisions.

In rising at this time for a brief
discussion of the resolution submitted by the lion. Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. MacLaren), I do so not with any idea of deferring the passing of the resolution, nor indeed of discussing its merits or demerits, because I realize that these can be discussed better when the definite and particular legislation based on the resolution is before the house. There are however two or three considerations that I think call for attention at the present time.
The resolution is divided into seven parts. It refers to the elimination of various provisions relating to the pension tribunal. This is not the time to discuss the pension tribunals, which have been functioning consequent on the legislation of 1930, but my own judgment, after mature observation, has been and is that the pension tribunals have been the best friends that the exservioemen of Canada have had since 1930. So I am indeed 
glad to hear the observation of the minister that in effect the pension tribunals are not being abolished but that their functions are being merged with those of the enlarged board of pension commissioners with their travelling quorums functioning in various parts of the dominion. That is the second part of the resolution.
The third refers to the continuation of .the pension appeal court as a court of appeal and review. I presume that new title has something to do with the institution of a new officer who is to be appointed under the terms of the legislation to be introduced.
The fourth provision is for the appointment of an administrative judge as a member of the appeal court. I think that provision will command 'the entire sympathy and support of this house.
The fifth is for the appointment of a travelling inspector of the veterans' bureau. That, I think, is one of the recommendations made by General Ross in part II of the excellent report submitted by him.
The sixth provision is for the appointment of pension counsel, who I understand, are to take over, in an altered form, some of the duties of the commission counsel appointed under the 1930 legislation. Speaking for myself, I am very glad indeed to see that the commission counsel are to be finally abolished. The appointment of a reviewing officer must be looked upon with a great deal of care by all members o,f this house, because as I understood the remarks of the minister, under the legislation to be introduced a single medical officer is to be appointed who is going to have complete power to advise the crown in regard to which cases should be appealed and which should not. I think this may be-I am not saying it is-giving to one individual powers of a very far-reaching and important Character.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
May I say that he will
be under the direction and control of the president of the pension appeal court.

Well, I
am not going to discuss details at the present time. I have every respect for the president of the pension appeal court, but to my mind that would be an objection to the reviewing officer. When an appeal is going to a judicial body, a court of final instance, and the president of that court has under his control the person who is to decide whether the appeal should go to that body for final judgment, I think there is a fundamental weakness there. However, I am not crticizing it at the present moment.

Pension Act
The seventh provision is for the payment of awards by the comptroller of the treasury; which, as I understand it, is transferring from the department the authority for paying pensions or awards made by the tribunals.
The history of pension legislation in this parliament ever since 1919 has been a very fortunate one indeed. It has been entirely removed from every suggestion of partisanship. We have had, I think, nine select committees of this parliament in various years considering all possible phases of pension administration. We had a royal commission under the chairmanship of my hon. friend the member for Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) who submitted to this parlia-men a most voluminous and excellent report upon which the legislation of 1923 was based; we had the legislation of 1930 resulting from the very excellent work of a committee presided over by my good friend the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). So if there have been mistakes in regard to the administration of the Pension Act they have not been intentional mistakes on the part of either side of the House of Commons. But the point which I rose to mention is that every single important revision of the Pension Act in previous sessions has been submitted to a committee of this House of Commons. Legislation based upon these seven provisions to which I have referred is to my mind nothing less than a complete recasting of the Pension Act. That act, as hon. members know, is one of the most complicated acts we have upon our statute books at the present time. I agree with my hon. friend the minister in regard to the splendid abilities of the gentlemen who formed that committee whose report I have before me, but we have now in this house an example of the consequences of introducing to this house a very complicated piece of legislation namely the railway bill. That bill is based on the report of a very eminent commission, yet we find a marked division of opinion among hon. gentlemen on all sides of the house in regard to its provisions. So I suggest to the hon. Minister of Pensions and National Health that before this bill is thrown into committee of the whole it should be referred to a committee of this house, not to hear further evidence, not to function as the committee whose report we have before us, but to examine the details of the bill, to call in experts, if they desire, either from the department or the associated veterans. But I think it is vital to the success of this legislation, in case there may be some controversial sections, not to have it thrown into committee of the whole without hon.
members on either side of the house being thoroughly familiar with it. In all sincerity, in the interest of the legislation and to preserve the nonpartisan attitude of former years, I suggest that when this bill is ready for presentation it be referred to a small committee of this house, of members thoroughly familiar with the details of pension administration and legislation, so that if possible we may have the unanimous judgment of the House of Commons in regard to what is to my mind one of the most important pieces of legislation in Canada.

I only wish to add a few words to what has been said by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie). As I understand it, although I have had no information with respect to the provisions of the bill, essentially it is to destroy and do away with the principal provisions of the pension legislation of 1930. I do not think it is my duty or that the burden should be placed upon me to defend that legislation, because it was passed unanimously by the committee that dealt with it; it was confirmed unanimously by this house and received the approbation of all soldier bodies throughout the country. I must say, however, that before taking away from that legislation its most important feature, namely the right of the returned soldier to have his day in court and to be heard by a tribunal as to the justice or otherwise of his case, we perhaps should have given the matter more consideration and should have had a more unanimous report.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is carefully preserved in the bill.

I am very glad to learn from the hon. gentleman who is in charge of the measure that this right is preserved in the bill, but I wonder why the pension tribunals are to be abolished. Is it simply because we wish to change the name? If that is the reason I do not know why so much fuss was made about this bill. If we are preserving the essential functions of the pension tribunals and simply changing their status, putting them under the board of pension commissioners instead of leaving them independent tribunals, then I think perhaps we have very strong reascti for opposing this bill. The tribunals and appeal courts were established in order to get away from the final jurisdiction of the board of pension commissioners, which in the minds of the soldiers throughout the country had not been functioning satisfactorily. After having read over the report
Pension Act

of the commission, which was composed of very able gentlemen, it appears to me that only a minority of the members recommended the action now proposed by the government. However, I will leave that point for discussion when the bill is brought before the house.
In support of what has been said by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), if the correct information has been given to us, namely that there will be some sixty or seventy sections in this proposed bill, I respectfully submit to the minister that it will be extremely difficult to discuss these sections in this House of Commons. There is no legislation on our statute books more complicated and more difficult of understanding to the lay mind-and to the legal mind as well-than the Pension Act. It requires constant study and application, and to throw this matter into the House of Commons without some preliminary study having been given to it will, I think, bring about the evil effects pointed out by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre. If the minister has not definitely made up his mind on that score I would ask him, in the interests of the legislation, in the interests of the soldier, and to keep to the practice followed hitherto in this house, to reconsider the matter and, if it is at all possible, form some small committee which need not hear witnesses but which could take means to be informed as to the reasons why these new sections are being introduced into the act. I very much fear that unless something of the kind is done we will have misunderstandings as to the purport of the legislation, and with all the goodwill in the world and the greatest desire to cooperate, which I am sure will be found on all sides of the house, those misunderstandings will occur.
There is one other matter to which I should like to direct attention, ll would ask the minister, and doubtless he will reply When we reach the committee stage, whether this bill will reduce the number of pensions granted to ex-soldiers or whether it will increase them; in other words I would ask whether the purport of this act is to be more generous or less generous to the ex-soldiers. If it is designed to save money I think perhaps the minister should tell us. If it is designed further to extend the application of pension^ and bring more returned men within the scope of the act I think we Should know it. As to the new machinery provided, I understand that eight or ten new pension commissioners are to be appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No, not ten new ones; there will be eight in all.
There are to be eight pension commissioners, so there will be five new members of the board.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No, four new ones.

There are three members at present and the chief medical officer? There will be four new members who will replace the eight or ten members of the present tribunals, and to that extent I am sure there will be a certain saving of the public money. Apart from that, however, I am at a loss to understand what saving there will be. If we are accomplishing this saving by placing the control of pensions once more under the jurisdiction of the board of pension commissioners I very much fear that this move will not give satisfaction, at any rate to the people most concerned, the returned soldiers.

With all due respect, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the speeches we have just heard from the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) and the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) show the utter futility of attempting to discuss something of which we know nothing. They surmised that the bill would contain something, and went on to say that in that event it would be right or wrong. If we are to take information we may gather, not surreptitiously but by conversation and discussion, and consider the resolution in that light we are not helping the measure in the slightest degree; we are only stirring up objections that perhaps will not otherwise come to the surface.
However, I do agree with one point brought up by each of the hon. members who spoke; that is, that we should consider very carefully the way we take up the provisions of this bill. This is a complicated matter; those of us who have had to do with pensions know that the provisions of the act are many and that often they are difficult to reconcile. It should be made as clear as possible, for it is a bill that we should have so plain that he who runs may read if that can be accomplished. It comes up for consideration by men who are not lawyers and who perhaps are not able to comprehend all its provisions, so I submit that we should use every effort to make it quite clear. I do not propose, however, to discuss hypothetically the provisions of this bill. There are many suggestions I might make at the moment, but I do commend to the very serious consideration of the minister the suggestion that every opportunity should

.CANADIAN NATIONAL-CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
The house resumed from Wednesday, April 19, consideration in committee of Bill No. 37, respecting the Canadian National Railways and to provide for cooperation with the Canadian Pacific Railway system and for other purposes-Mr. Manion-Mr. Hanson (York^Sunbury) in the chair.

We are dealing with section 16,
subsection 1.

When the committee
rose last evening it was discussing an amendment which had been suggested by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. At that time I pointed out that I felt the amendment did not go far enough. The latter part of this subsection reads:
They are further directed that whenever they shall so agree they Shall endeavour to provide, as part of such measure, plan or arrangement or otherwise, for a fair and reasonable apportionment as between the employees of National railways and Pacific railways, respectively, of such employment as may be incident to the operation of such measure, plan or. arrangement.
That subsection refers to ithe amalgamation of services, whether the running of trains, the operation of shops and stations, or whatever it may be. It will be noticed that the question of the allocation of employment is left to the officers of the two railway companies with the direction that they shall endeavour to provide for equitable distribution of employment. It seems to me that if the interests of the railway employees are to be protected, something will have to he included in .this section to make the equitable distribution of employment obligatory or binding. Many years ago I had some experience in these matters, although in a much less complicated form. In those days the railways were taking over other small lines to incorporate in their general operations and the question as to ho.w the employees of the small lines were to be dealt with was constantly coming up for consideration. In a case of this kind it would be impossible, under the agreements existing at present between the employees and the railway companies, for the management of the roads to

do the things suggested by this section. There should be some obligatory provision to provide for the proper allocation of employment.
Let me give one or two illustrations. It might be decided that the Canadian National shops and the Canadian Pacific shops in Ottawa be amalgamated. I am not suggesting that that will happen, but it is a possibility. The work would be concentrated in one seit of shops and there is now no authority vested in the officials of the railways to take employees from the National shops and put them into 'the Pacific shops, or vice versa. This could not be done as long as there were sufficient employees on the lists of the one company to do all 'the work involved. Another illustration would be in the running of trains, say from Ottawa to Toronto or Montreal. One train might be taken off leaving the other train running over the line of the other railway to do all the work. Let us assume that the train left would run over the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The officials of the railways cannot decade that two Canadian National and two Canadian Pacific crews will be utilized. Under the agreements now existing, 'the Canadian Pacific men would 'have the ultimate decision. The same would apply to the Canadian National if it were decided to run the train over that line.
It seems to me that if there is to be equitable distribution of employment, some plan must be worked out by which a representative of the men will be clothed with authority to allocate the work upon some basis of seniority or percentage; otherwise, we will be having a continuous dispute between the employees of the two roads and injustices will certainly be done. I feel that the words "endeavour to provide" should be struck out and "shall provide" substituted therefor. There should also be an added clause to provide that the accredited representatives of each class of employee concerned would have authority to allocate employment equitably between the several classes of men involved. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is more directly involved in this matter and has been more recently concerned than I have been, and I expected that he would have brought forward an amendment which would cover this point. Unless these things are provided for, I believe there will be a very serious effect upon the employees of the railways.
Does not the hon. member think that the word "respectively" in line 15 provides for distribution as between the two companies?

My point is that under the agreements existing between the companies and the men, the companies have no authority to do any such thing as is herein provided. If two shops at any terminal are brought together and all the work of the two railways is to be done in a National railway shop, so long as there were sufficient employees on the list, perhaps not in active employment-there are hundreds of men on the list who are not now in employment-they would have first preference in getting a job and taking extra work before a single man could be transferred from the other shop, and any who were transferred would come in as new employees altogether under existing arrangements. The same is true with regard to train service men, bridge men, track men and any other class of employee covered under the agreements now in existence. The agreements as between the employees of one company and the employees of the other are vastly different, covering different districts, and varying as to seniority rights and all that sort of thing. If the bill is left in its present form there will be utter and complete confusion and the interests of the men will not be properly taken care of.

May I observe to the committee
that we are discussing subclause 1 of clause 16, to which an amendment was proposed yesterday by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, which I understand was not put. I 3hall now read it. It is moved by Mr. Heenan that subclause 1 of section 16 be amended by adding after the word "arrangement" in line 17 the words:
But in no event shall such measure, plan or arrangement become operative until the representatives of the employees affected have been given sixty days' notice.

If there is no
objection at this stage I was going to make some observations on the question of compulsory cooperation. I wonder if the minister or the Prime Minister would entertain the idea, if they feel so strongly on the question of compulsory cooperation, of having a clause providing for it inserted in the bill, but providing also that it shall not come into effect at present or until they think it is desirable, and then only upon proclamation by the governor in council. I may say that I have put bills of that nature through the Saskatchewan provincial house, and also through this house. We wanted a provision of that nature in certain acts, but we did not know whether it would be required or not, and so we in-

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

serted it and then provided that it would only be brought into effect by proclamation.
The reason I make this suggestion is twofold. Out in the west we have been fed up, if I may use that term, on the policy enunciated by some of the members of the wheat pool favouring compulsory cooperation. To a great many of the contract signers of the pool such a policy was abhorrent, so muoh so that they started up an organization against it and defeated it, and that was the end of that campaign. The case might not be wholly parallel to this one, but nevertheless some of us feel quite strongly that so long as the two railways are doing such excellent work in the way of cooperation as they are at the present time, even though it as under the disciplining effect of the times, it might be wiser to let them run along just as they are doing, but always conscious of the fact that there is a provision in the law that the government may at any time in their wisdom invoke the provision for compulsory cooperation if the railways do not continue their good work in voluntarily cooperating. Such a course would be very gratifying to myself. I have no authority to speak for anybody else. The thought has just come to me now, and I make that suggestion. If it will not work in this case I shall be glad to be enlightened as to why it will not work, but if it will work I think it would help to bridge quite a gulf between this side of the house and the ministerial benches.
To repeat, my suggestion is that the principle of compulsory cooperation be inserted in the law but that it foe invoked only by proclamation at the instance of the government, and in the meantime let the railway companies run along as they are doing mow. They are doing magnificently, as was so eloquently and forcibly described by the minister in his very first speech on this subject. Why spoil that splendid work of voluntary cooperation by saying, "You must cooperate," when they are already doing it? You know bow cranky and cussed human nature naturally is, and how you hate to be told to do a thing when you are doing it. That is very much the ease here. The railways are being told by law that they must cooperate when everybody testifies that they are cooperating magnificently now in a voluntary way. As a matter of diplomacy, as a matter of gratifying that trait of human nature that exists in all of us, and in some more than others, it seems to me that it would be the part of wisdom, as well as good parliamentary tactics in connection with this knotty question, to adopt such a course as I have suggested. I

admit that I am against compulsory cooperation. The courts in Saskatchewan have decided that there "ain't mo such critter," if I may use that language and not attribute it to the bench. Injunctions have been taken out on the ground that compulsory cooperation was contradictory in its terms, and judgment has been given accordingly. So I have authority for my view. Unfortunately I have not the judgment here, but it was given by no less a judge than a member of the appeal court of Saskatchewan. With that as my authority, and with my experience of 'the terrible conflict that ran for years' through the farmers in the wheat pool on the subject of compulsion, I say that there is something fundamentally unsound and undesirable in the principle of compulsory cooperation. If the railways will noit cooperate, then as a last resort the government can say: We shall have regretfully to invoke this compulsory feature which has been provided in the law.
I have no motion to make, Mr. Chairman. I am simply making this suggestion. Maybe it is no good at all, but I know that it has worked out in both provincial and federal legislation. On one occasion we had to invoke the clause, and in the other case we did not. That is all! I have to say at the moment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The suggestion which has been made by the hon. gentleman regarding the adding of a clause to the bill providing that Part III shall not come into force except by proclamation has been considered in another chamber, with the result that it was not favourably entertained-

It was discussed
there?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. The vote against it was very small, only one, I think; I am speaking subject to correction.
Pretty close, but I had not heard of it previously.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the observations made by the hon. gentleman are worthy of every consideration.
This affords me the opportunity to say that there has been some misapprehension on the part of many people as to the effect of this part of the bill. Some have thought that this was a provision in the law to dragoon the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway, or the corporation as such, to do what they did not want to do regardless of what the views of the shareholders might be. Now, first of all, the law provides that whatever action is to be taken is action that is favour-

able to both roads. That is, it must be of benefit to both in the minds at least of those responsible for the setting up of the tribunal.
Secondly, a tribunal will never be set up unless there is a difference of opinion between the two roads as to whether or not it is desirable to do some particular thing. One road may think that the- benefits that will result from taking a given course are not anything like what have been suggested by the other road; the other road may think that the benefits may be very great. It is not compulsion in the ordinary sense of the term, but an arbitration between two contending views-the view of one company that the benefits would be very great, and the view of the other that the benefits would be, we will say, very trifling. In such an event a tribunal may be set up in the manner provided by the act to arbitrate, to resolve and determine the differences between the two roads.
As I see it at the moment, in view of what the hon. gentleman has said and in view of what has been said by others, the suggestion that compulsory arbitration should not be provided for in the bill except by proclamation would merely mean that when a difference arose that was so acute that it could not be disposed of by compromise between the contending parties, an arbitral tribunal should be set up to resolve that difficulty. The suggestion is worthy of every consideration. Between now and Monday, namely on Saturday, when there is an opportunity to consider these matters in full, the council will carefully consider what has been said. It may be that possibly in view of the strong opinion expressed by the hon. member, and by others who have discussed the matter in another chamber, such action should be taken. We will give it every consideration. At any rate debate is not closed on the section.

Lest the opinion expressed
by the hon. member for MelviLle should appear to be the opinion of all hon. members on this side of the house, may I say-and I am not doing so out of factious opposition- that the arbitral tribunal feature commended itself most to me when I voted for the second reading of the bill. I do believe if there is anything in the legislation worthy of being retained, it is exactly that provision.
Mr. BEiNNETT:	This will Tetain it. It
is only a question of when the law becomes effective.

I am not making this statement wiit'h a view to being disagreeable or indulging in any carping criticism, but it 53719-2591
seems to me that a tribunal which would be set up more or less automatically on the application of one or other of the railroads would be more in the interests of both railroads than one set up by proclamation of the government. Such a tribunal would be more in the interests of the government itself, and those of the railroads.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
To correct my hon.
friend, may I say that the tribunal would not be set up by proclamation; the law would become effective to enable it to be set up.

On that point may I ask
this question: If the government should adopt the suggestion made by the hon. member for Melville, would it then by proclamation bring into being a tribunal each time a dispute arose, or once they proclaimed the act in farce would it be in force from that time forward? It would mot be proclaimed at intervals?

Unless it were framed in

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
And that would be a
very difficult thing to do. The statute would at once become effective, and be binding for the future. The tribunals, of course, are separate tribunals with respect to each dispute. I may say that giving the matter my own personal view I was of the opinion that it was not desirable to provide for it coming into- force by proclamation. In that respect I shared the view 'held by the hon. member for Quebec South. However, I have listened to a great many arguments, including that of the hon. member for Melville, as to the desirability of having it come into force by proclamation. As I have said, my personal view was the other way. .

Yesterday afternoon I
showed that section 5 of the bill -is mot in accordance with the report of the royal commission, and that there is nothing in that report with regard to the removal from office of the trustees, as stipulated in section 7 of the third draft of the bill. Therefore the government cannot pretend that the bill is entirely in accordance with the report.
In regard to section 16 of the bill the report of the royal commission at paragraph 210 is as follows:
We have emphasized the fact that a principal weakness of the past decade has been the failure of the railways to act together in their own interests and in the interests of the public. Jt is not enough that each should take all practicable measures of economy in respect of
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

This clause deals with the question of men who are likely to be laid off and those who are retained in the service of the railway companies. It directs the companies to make a fair apportionment of the services of men as between the two companies, in case of consolidation of services. Now the first question that arises is: What is a fair apportionment of such employment? Secondly, who is to be responsible for making this apportionment? If this house enacts legislation to create a tribunal or direct a body to make this division of labour, then I am afraid we will get into great difficulties. Personally I think that the less we have to do with 'this question of apportionment the better it will be, because any legislation that we enact, especially in view of the fact that there are in existence agreements between the railway companies and their men, is bound to get us into difficulties either between the railway companies or between the companies and the men or between ourselves and the employees. So, personally, I would rather leave the question to the companies and the organizations of the men affected; in that way I think we may save ourselves a great deal of trouble. If we take any action we then become responsible for the apportionment. If we had not faith in the men's organizations or the companies to do the fair thing in this respect this might be a proper body to make provision that a fair apportionment be made. But at present the men are satisfied that they can depend on their organizations to do what is right, and therefore I would rather see the matter left in the simplest form possible to save future embarrassment.
Perhaps the minister may have in his possession now -particulars of the method by which the apportionment was made in the case of the recent pooling of train services between Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa. That may give some idea how the thing was worked.

I heartily agree with the remarks of the last speaker. I believe that as
the clause is framed it protects the men of both companies as far as it is possible for this legislation to protect them. I have given the matter further consideration since the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) moved his resolution; I have listened to my hon. friend from East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson); I have discussed it with railway men and I am informed that to leave it as it is would be the most practical way of getting beneficial results for those concerned. This may be pointed out, that the two companies-	*
are further directed that whenever they shall so agree-
On cooperative measures.
-they shall endeavour to provide, as part of such measure, plan or arrangement or otherwise, for a fair and reasonable apportionment as between the employees of National railways and Pacific railways, respectively, of such employment as may be incident to the operation of such measure, plan or arrangement.
So the companies are directed to endeavour to see that their employees get a fair and equitable apportionment of the employment, and I know enough about the management of the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National to know that both managements are very jealous of the rights of their men and would do everything in their power to see that the employment that remains, if there be some curtailment, would be fairly and equitably divided. I think to attempt to make the clause any stronger would really complicate' it so that it would be very difficult of oj)or-ation.
My hon. friend the member for Kenora-Rainy River moved an amendment yesterday:
But in no event shall such measure, plan, or arrangement become operative until the representatives of the employees affected have been given sixty days' notice.
I submit that the amendment would hold up the review of any forms of attempted cooperation by the two railways and would not accomplish the end desired to any greater extent than the clause already in the bill.
There is still another point to remember; it is that there may be and no doubt will be forms of cooperation which will save money otherwise than at the expense of the men. Let me explain that by an illustration. Let us suppose two pick-up lines are serving practically the same territory, and we have many cases of that kind in this country. It is decided to abandon one of the lines and both railways are given running rights over the remaining line, without diminishing the number of trains at all. There the saving would be in the cost of maintaining that section of track which was abandoned. It is.
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

true that a certain number of men in the section gangs might be let go, but after all there are other matters in connection with maintenance than pick and shovel work; there is the matter of rails, the ties and so on, and a considerable saving would be made. So after listening to the whole discussion I submit with all respect that the clause which has been inserted in the act will accomplish the end desired. My hon. friend from North Winnipeg asked about the arrangement made in regard to the amalgamation of the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk and the Intercolonial with the Canadian National.

No, I was referring to the
more recent consolidation of services between Montreal and Toronto and Ottawa and Toronto; I thought perhaps the minister might have some information as to how the men were dealt with in that case and what apportionment of labour was made.

I am sorry 1 have not that information; I thought my hon. friend was referring to the original coordination of the different portions of the Canadian National system. My submission is that under this provision, when there had to be a decrease in the number of men each railway would get an equal proportion of the jobs remaining, and those men would be appointed in accordance with their seniority. As my hon. friend pointed out, the seniority of the men is arranged between the unions and the railway companies, so it would merely be a matter of taking the men in the regular order of seniority. The senior men on one line would not prevail over the junior men on the other. If fifty men were to be kept employed on each railway the fifty senior men on the Canadian Pacific and the fifty senior men on the Canadian National would be retained. I think that is all provided for in the act, and I trust that my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River and my hon. friend from East Algoma will accept that provision. I may add, however, that if after the act has been in force for some time it should be found that any injustice was being done that could be remedied by this house, most assuredly I would be one of those to ask that action be taken. I come from a railway city which is served by both lines, and I am most anxious to see that the railway men get justice and a fair deal so far as it is possible to accord it by this act.

I am still assuming that
the minister is sincere in his desire to understand all the complications that really arise with regard to seniority rights. I could give
TMr. Manion.]
an illustration to show that the case cited by the minister might not work out at all. We might have the two railways running side by side, and when it is decided to abandon one line the railway companies will apportion the employment. The minister says the men will be taken by seniority, and I think probably a good many people who are not acquainted with these complications would look upon it as the minister does. But let us suppose that all the men on one of the lines were senior to all the men on the other line. Then the junior men could not get in at all.

I think my hon. friend misunderstands the clause, because it provides that the employment will be divided. I pointed out a moment ago that the senior men on one road would not prevail over the junior men on the other; that the intent of the act is that the men retained on the portion of the road operated jointly, or whatever the case may be, should be divided equally between the two roads. The senior men on the Canadian Pacific would get their proportion of employment and the senior men on the Canadian National would get their proportion.

This shows the difficulty
of legislating along these lines. In that case we would have the junior men of one line coming in to displace the senior men of another line in that particular district. I submit to the minister that this is a complication that cannot be dealt with by legislation, and that is why I submitted my amendment. If it is carried out it will not cost the railroad companies or the government a dollar. Let me point out. to the minister once more just what we are doing. Here we are doing something by legislation which I never heard of before; the railway companies themselves, without consultation with the railway employees, will apportion the employment. According to an act- of parliament the railway companies can dovetail these men as they wish. A short time ago the minister stated that he had consulted some railway men in this regard. I do not know whether he meant the representatives of the employees, but I have in my hand a letter that was sent to Right Hon. Arthur Meighen when this' bill was in the Senate, and this is one of the provisions requested in that letter. It also asks for compensation for employees who may lose their jobs and for other matters with which I have not dealt, because the amendment of the hon. member for North Winnipeg with regard to compensation was declared out of order. Therefore I have only suggested that

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
when any cooperative arrangement is considered, it shall not become operative until the representatives of the men have had sixty days notice. I think I know enough about railroad operation to feel sure that in these cases the companies know what they are going to do two or three months ahead of time. All I want is some provision in this act under which the companies shall advise the railway men of what is going to happen so that they may get together and consult with the management as to what is fair and reasonable.
There are some other points, to which I should like to direct the attention of the minister, which may not 'have occurred to him. This is a gigantic problem; I am glad he is looking after it instead of myself, because I am sure he will make a better job of it. Even where there are running rights over different sections of the railways, because of our gre>aiter motive power and the greater capacity of our rolling stock we will not require so many trains; they will be hauling greater tonnage and there will not be so many men employed. I think it must be taken for granted that after this legislation is passed the train crews all through Canada can give up all thought of operating with much less than full tonnage. There will be a saving in that to the country and the companies, but undoubtedly fewer men will be required, and I want to provide that where these men are to be changed from one pant of the country to another or to be dovetailed in the matter of seniority the government should grant them at least sixty days' notice to kiss their families goodbye.
An bon. MEMBER: Too long.

Some of the single men
think sixty days too long. If we sentence a man to be hanged in this country we give him a few months to make peace with the world, but here we are providing for the slaughter of thirty or forty thousand men and the minister is refusing to .give them sixty days' notice. In this amendment I am not asking for compensation, so 'that my amendment is fair and reasonable. Suppose we adopted a system of compensation as between Canadian National and Canadian Pacific employees. We close shops in Halifax or Winnipeg on the Canadian National and operate Canadian Pacific shops. How are we to dovetail the men into seniority districts? How are you going to pay the pensions of these men? Take an example? Suppose you closed the Canadian National shops in one part of t'he country and transferred some of the employees to Canadian Pacific Railway shops.
Who would pay them? W'ho would make provision for their pensions-because some might be on the verge of acquiring pension. These are matters that can be. dealt with only between the men and the companies. Having regard to all the adjustments that they make between themselves, I am satisfied that these things could be satisfactorily disposed of much better between the men and the company affected than on the floor of this house. This bill provides that the companies shall do this without any consultation at all with the men; t'he men have not a word to say in the matter. I would point out to the minister that this is an act of parliament and not an ordinary agreement, and I would again ask him in all fairness to give some consideration to this amendment. I am satisfied that if it were accepted it would iron out a whole lot of troubles in the future.

I have no desire to be at all stubborn in dealing with the hon. gentleman's amendment, but I do not think it would advance the interests of the men. If it would do that I should be agreeable to it, but my best information is that it does not in any way protect them; on the contrary, it only complicates the legislation. At this very moment, while this legislation is being considered, before it has become law, the cooperative measures which we are now supporting are being carried on just as they have been for some years, though not to the extent that we should have liked.
Why bother with this legislation then?

Because the railways did not cooperate on a sufficiently extensive scale. That was the opinion of the Duff commission and it is equally mine. As soon as we came into power both the Prime Minister and I advised the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific to cooperate more fully than they had done in the past, and they promised to do so. They did not do so however, each blaming the other for the lack of cooperation. That was the report I received, and the Prime Minister was informed likewise whenever the officers were spoken to about it. Each claimed that the other wanted the big share of the benefits accruing from the proposed cooperation. At this very time such cooperative measures are being taken, and arrangements with regard to employment are now in the hands of the union. I think my hon. friend will agree that when there is a dispute between one of the railways and the men as to seniority the union of the railway employees
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

concerned have a right to interview the officers of the company and argue the case, and in the last resort they now have the right to ask for a conciliation board. I think therefore that the men are amply protected. I do not see that my hon. friend's amendment would do more than complicate the measure and for that reason I regret that I cannot accept it.

I agree that the men are cooperating with the railways as they have done before, but I want to point out again to the minister that there is not now in force, nor has there ever been in force an act of parliament that precluded them from negotiating. Now, however, we are passing an act that practically precludes the men from having any say in the matter. It is provided that the railway companies shall make provision for a fair and reasonable apportionment. This is an act of parliament, and it makes all the difference. Prior to this time the men did cooperate and they would do so in the future were it not for the fact that we are now passing an act that precludes them from having any say.
This does not interfere with agreements between the men and the railways.

I am trying to point it
out to the minister; it may take me a long time to do so but I think it is important that the minister should grasp the significance of it. The agreements between the railways and the men are agreements between the men and the individual company-an agreement, for instance, between the Canadian National and Canadian National men, or the Canadian Pacific and Canadian Pacific employees. In this bill we are giving running rights and providing for dovetailing and the merging of services, something entirely different from anything we have had before. Formerly it was an easy matter when a station was to be abandoned, or anything of that kind, for the men to get together with the company and make an adjustment; but now we are going to have Canadian National services merged with Canadian Pacific in some parts of the country and vice versa, and there is no agreement existing that safeguards the interests of the men in this regard. The more I think of it the more necessary an amendment such as I propose appears to be. What possible injurious effect could it have? When the railway companies are going to merge services or dovetail men or abandon some service, ought they not to give the men notice? What possible harm could that have? 
All they have to do is to advise the representatives of the men, as they have done for the last fifty years, that so and so is going to be done.
If I understand the amendment correctly the gist of it is that the men should be given sixty days' notice or sixty days' pay.
No, that is not the amendment.
Well, sixty days' pay in lieu of their services if they are not required.

No. I want the hon.
member to understand my amendment. I am not talking about pay or compensation. There are certain things here which the railways have a right to do with regard to new companies, leases, entrusting agreements, or licences, or agreements for the pooling and division of earnings arising from the joint operation of any part or parts of freight or passenger traffic, or express, telegraph or other operating activities or services, joint trackage, running rights and so on. I am asking that the representatives of these men be given sixty days' notice before these measures are put into operation.

Just what has my hon.
friend in mind? He has mentioned certain things which I am sure his amendment does not cover.

If the hon. member will
look at section 16-
I have followed the section with my hon. friend.

-he will find that it reads:
Without restricting the generality of the foregoing, any such measures, plans or arrangements may include and be effected by means of-

From Mr. Hunger-ford, of the Canadian National, and Mr. Grant Hall, of the Canadian Pacific, down the line of officers, the management in both companies deal with the men because the directors do not understand the complications of the agreements between the unions and the companies. Generally speaking, disputes between individual men and the company concerned go no higher than Mr. Hungerford as vicepresident and general manager of the Canadian National and Mr. Grant Hall, vicepresident and general manager of the Canadian Pacific. Neither the trustees nor the directors would be capable of dealing with such questions and that is one of the reasons I have endeavoured to keep away from such matters.

After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Just before six o'clock the minister told us that when an employee had any complaint to make, it was referred to the management of the railway through the brotherhood. However, there are some employees who do not belong to a brotherhood. In certain parts of the country, especially along the old Intercolonial, railway employees are in the habit of coming to their member of parliament for assistance in cases of trouble. This afternoon the hon. member for East Algoma referred to human nature. Men are not perfect and they sometimes make little mistakes. I do not consider it to be political interference for a member of parliament to intervene with the management on behalf of an employee who has been charged with drunkenness or something of that kind. I have followed this practice ever since I was elected and I am not ashamed of it. These men have always come to me for assistance, and it never made any difference whether they were Liberals or Conservatives. I investigated their cases and drew up briefs to be submitted to the management. I was not always rewarded with gratitude but I felt I was doing only my duty. The only time I was ever insulted during an election was once by a Tory whom I had had reinstated in the employ of the railway. I recall another instance where a man was

accused of being drunk while on duty. I went with him to see the superintendent who gave him a calling down and he was finally reinstated because of his family and upon the promise of behaviour in the future. On the station platform he wanted to kiss my hand after he found he was to be reinstated, but I would not stand for such a demonstration. But a few months afterwards he voted against me.

He kissed someone
else.

I recall another instance
where I had a man reinstated and when I visited the polls in my home town I found him representing my opponent. Some years ago there was a rumour that the shops at Riviere du Loup would be closed. I at once wrote to the former Minister of Railways, Mr. Dunning, and stated that I would object very strongly to the reengagement of Sir Henry Thornton if my people did not receive justice. I sent copies of that letter to the members of the cabinet. I met Sir Henry Thornton in Montreal with Mr. Hungerford and Mr. Appleton and in my presence Sir Henry told Mr. Appleton that I should have justice. After several trips to Montreal I was able to find out definitely that the shops would not be closed.
There was another man who had twelve or fourteen complaints made against him. This man had been most unfair to me upon a previous occasion but when he came to me for assistance I wrote to the management. Because of the numerous complaints, the management did not feel like reinstating him. He telephoned me to ask for another recommendation. I refused to give it to him, but immediately sent one to a friend of mine who lived in his vicinity and told him to tell the man not to speak to me again but that I was ready to assist him provided that such assistance was asked for by someone else. Every member of parliament should be ready to assist any railway employee who is in trouble or who has not been treated fairly either by the brotherhood or by the management. I do not intend to recite all the cases of injustice to railway employees in my district but in endeavouring to help these men I have made no difference between Conservatives and Liberals.
When a man once has a job, every effort should be made to see that he retains it. When an opening occurs we can favour our political friends, but I do not think any effort should be made to replace a man already in a position. These men rely upon ["Mr. Pouliot.]
their jobs for their living and they should not be displaced because of political considerations.
I do not intend to propose any amendment before asking the minister if he would accept an amendment to section 16 to provide that the trustees shall investigate and reconsider every case submitted to them by a member of parliament.

I do not think it would be
possible for the trustees to do that because it would mean that their whole time would be taken up in the consideration of these cases. During the last three years since I have been minister I have received complaints practically every day from -men who felt they were not getting a fair deal from either their own union, some other union or the management of the railway. It is the duty of the managing officers of the railway to consider such cases. I do not think the trustees should be asked to deal with matters of this kind. I have no reason to believe that the officers of either railway have any desire to do other than to give the fairest consideration to every case with which they have to deal. Of course the personal equation enters into the matter but I do not believe they have any desire to be unfair. I am sorry I cannot offer any encouragement to my hon. friend in regard to the matter he discusses because I do not think it would be fair to the trustees. I believe it would detract from the possibility of their doing good work from a business standpoint for the Canadian National Railways.

I quite agree with the minister, that it is an absolute impossibility for this parliament to interfere with the seniority rights of the railway men. They have their agreements and the necessary machinery to deal with a matter of that kind. Reading the clause before us as it stands, I do not think it means anything, and I believe that something is needed along the lines of the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River to give what I consider very necessary protection to the men who might be involved in any cooperative effort by the railways of this country. The section is not mandatory. It simply says that they shall endeavour to provide as a part of such measure, plan or arrangement, for a fair and reasonable apportionment as between the employees of the National railway and the Pacific railway. In my judgment that would place too much power in the hands of the management. The amendment gives the necessary opportunity

to the men's representatives to meet with the management, and if necessary have a board of conciliation set up.
It is absolutely essential that there should be a clear definition of the rights of the men in this regard. The way I const-rue the section is that the railways themselves have absolute power, and can ignore the existing arrangements between the men and the railways, because, since this is an act of parliament, it would take precedence even over the award of a board of conciliation. The minister would be well advised to incorporate in this section the idea expressed in the amendment of the member for Kenora-Rainy River. From my practical experience in many years of negotiating agreements between men and employers I can say that the question of seniority rights stands oust even above that of wages. Men are deeply concerned over their seniority rights and more trouble is experienced in negotiating the seniority rights of the men than in negotiating wages and working conditions. I think we should see to it that these rights are protected prior to the passage of this bill into law. I am not unmindful of what the minister said this afternoon- that in the practical application of this legislation amendments may be found necessary, but I would rather see the amendments made n-ow than take a chance on making them after the railways have probably got into difficulties with the employees over this particular section.

I had hoped that after the recess the minister would have been in a position to say that he accepted both the amendment and the amendment to the amendment, because I think it is only fair and reasonable. The amendment provides that the men shall receive sixty days' notice in any readjustment of the railway services in this country. It is quite evident from the silence of the minister, however, that the government is not prepared to accept the amendment; consequently I hope that more members on this side of the house wall take part in the discussion in appealing to the government for a square deal for the railroad men of this country.
Here we are with a measure before us that contemplates throwing out of employment thousands of railroad men, and yet the minister and the government practically refuse, or have done so up to the present, to allow the men to be given notice so that they can readjust their working arrangements with the company. I wonder if the minister is not now prepared to close me off by saying that he will accept my amendment even though he reduces the sixty days to fifty, or even 5371&-2601

Fooling the public! It is a bill to fool the public of Canada, because it is an amalgamation. The minister says that the railroads always treated their men well. How are you going to dovetail these men in according to seniority unless the men sit down and agree with the company? Who is going to decide whether the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific is to be responsible for the payment of those men's wages? I shall now try to come down from the heights that the two gladiators attained. Last week end I travelled on one of the new pooled trains to Toronto. Previously the service of the Canadian National Railways to Toronto was one of the finest in the country. It used to be a crack train running over a crack track.
It cracked our purses.

But a great dbange has taken place, and I was wondering if that change was brought about by voluntary action. If it was, it says a whole lot for our national railway officers. Now there is a mixed train made up of one coach, one baggage car and about fifty freight cars to be distributed between here and Toronto. It took four hours to cover the distance from Ottawa to Portland formerly covered in less than two. How long does the railway expect to retain passenger traffic with such a service as that? Unless something is done the remnant of passenger and small freight traffic will soon be lost to the buses and trucks. They see the heads of their fellow labourers dropping into the basket one after the other like apples falling off a tree. Surely it would be only humane and considerate to give some notice when making these dismissals. The hon. member asked for sixty days notice; if we cannot get sixty, give us fifty or forty.
In all sections of the country where the service has been reduced to a mixed train three times a week, the railways will get precious little passenger or light freight traffic with a service like that, without installing a railway bus and truck sei'vice themselves. Our object is to try to make this 'bill as little objectionable as possible, as it is bound to go through and receive royal assent. Suppose the Canadian Pacific concludes to operate a bus and truck service in an effort to catch the remaining express and light traffic available; the Canadian National will want to do the same. I am not sure whether the inauguration of such a service by the national railways would be classed as capital expenditure, but if so they would have to come to the government before the expenditure could be made. If it is not considered as a capital expenditure, they will have to go to the trustees for authority to invest money in a service of this kind. The trustees will have the authority to refuse, and if they do refuse-and this possibility is not imaginary-the freight and passenger traffic will gravitate to the buses and trucks operated by the Canadian Pacific. On section 19-Hearings to be held in matters of substantial public concern.

This section states:
If, in the opinion of the presiding officer of any tribunal, any application made to him raises matters of substantial concern to the public or a section of the public, he may direct-
Remembering the powers that are given the arbitral tribunal, does the minister not think this section should state that the presiding officer shall give notice in some way, perhaps through the press, of matters of public concern? I do not want to reiterate again and again the powers of this tribunal, but surely it should not be left to the opinion of the chairman as to whether or not a particular matter concerns the public. I have in mind the possibility that some service may be abandoned which would affect those living along that line. This could be done bv the tribunal without notice to the public and without the people situated along that line having the right to submit their argument to the tribunal. I think already the presiding officer has more power than he should have, and surely he ought not to have in addition the power to determine whether or not a certain matter is of public interest. I think we should make it mandatory on the presiding officer to make public the applications coming before the tribunal.

A portion of this clause is mandatory; if the hon. gentleman reads subsection 2 he will see that where the matter affects the province the presiding officer must notify the attorney general of that province. It is true that in other cases it is left to the opinion of the presiding officer, but after all
we must give the chairman of such an important tribunal credit for being reasonable, and we must believe that he would give a just and fair decision in a matter affecting any section of the public. I do not think we need argue because the matter is left in his hands to a certain extent. Probably many cases will come up in which it will not be necessary to hold public hearings because there will be no other interest involved than the two companies. I think we can safely leave it in the hands of the man who is appointed to that important position, especially since no abandonment can take place without the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners. As my hon. friend knows, that is an amendment we will move a little later.

I must confess that I rather agree with the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. I think the minister was quite right when he said that many cases, perhaps the majority, may be left to the discretion of the presiding officer, but even in section 2 I see the words:
-which in the opinion of the presiding officer specially affects any province of Canada-
So it is not mandatory; it is left to his discretion, both as to whether the matter is of public interest and as to whether representations shall be received. Certainly I think that in important matters it should be possible for those interested to make representations on behalf of interested parties. It seems to me that we are giving very wide discretionary powers to the chairman of the tribunal. I am quite prepared to give him wide powers, but it seems to me that here we are going almost too far when we leave it to him to decide whether or not the hearing shall be public and whether or not any representations shall be made. I can quite conceive that in this work of cooperation many matters may come up of very great interest not only to the railways but to other parties as well, and I think some provision should be included by which interested parties should be able to make representations where that seems advisable.

I think that is the intention of the act. My hon. friend must remember that the chairman of the tribunal is not interested in either of the companies; he is in a position of independence. He has no interest in concealing any of these applications from the public. He is placed there in a judicial capacity, if you like, representing the public, so that he will have every interest in protecting the public. I am informed that
